docs.title: Digital Logic Lab: Behavioral Modeling and Seven-Segment Displays
Objectives
docs.text:
• Master behavioral modeling for combinational logic using Verilog always blocks.
  • Master the use of if-else and case statements.
  • Understand how the seven-segment displays on the EGO1 development board operate.
  • Design a BCD-to-seven-segment decoder and verify it on the board.

docs.title: 1.1 What Is Behavioral Modeling?
docs.text: Behavioral modeling is a higher level of abstraction than structural modeling (connecting basic gates) and dataflow modeling (writing Boolean expressions). Like a high-level programming language such as C, it implements a function by describing the circuit's behavior and algorithm. The synthesis tool automatically infers the underlying logic-gate circuit.

docs.title: 1.2 The always Block for Combinational Logic
docs.text:
In Verilog, behavioral modeling is primarily expressed through always blocks. For combinational logic, use always @(*).

  • Syntax:

Verilog

always @(*) begin
    // 行为级描述语句 (if-else, case等)
end

  • Key characteristics (common sources of mistakes—remember these):

  • @(*) is the sensitivity list. It means that the always block is triggered whenever any input signal referenced on the right-hand side of an assignment within the block changes.

  • A variable assigned on the left-hand side must be declared as type reg. This is a language requirement. In combinational logic, the synthesized hardware is still a connection rather than a physical register.

docs.title: 1.3 Comparing assign and always @(*)
docs.text: Criterion Dataflow Modeling (assign) Behavioral Modeling (always @(*)) Assignment target type Must be wire Must be reg Typical use Simple logic expressions and connections Complex decisions, multiplexers, and decoders Supported constructs Conditional operator ? : if-else, case, and for loops

docs.title: 2.1 The if-else Statement
docs.text:
As in C, an if-else statement expresses prioritized conditional logic.

Verilog

always @(*) begin
    if (sel == 2'b00) begin
        out = a;
    end else if (sel == 2'b01) begin
        out = b;
    end else begin
        out = c;
    end
end

Important: An if-else statement used for combinational logic must include an else branch. Otherwise, the synthesis tool infers an additional latch, which can cause serious timing problems in the implemented hardware.

docs.title: 2.2 The case Statement
docs.text:
A case statement selects among multiple branches and is commonly used in multiplexers, decoders, and state machines. The branches do not have priorities; they are evaluated in parallel.

Verilog

always @(*) begin
    case (sel)
        2'b00: out = a;
        2'b01: out = b;
        2'b10: out = c;
        2'b11: out = d;
        default: out = 1'b0; // 必须加上 default，防止产生 Latch！
    endcase
end

Important: A case statement must include a default branch. Otherwise, the synthesis tool infers an additional latch, which can cause serious timing problems in the implemented hardware.

docs.title: 3. Seven-Segment Display Operation on the EGO1
3.1 Hardware Principles
docs.text:
A seven-segment display consists of seven bar-shaped light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and one dot-shaped LED for the decimal point (DP). Different combinations of illuminated LEDs display the digits 0–9 and selected letters.

According to the EGO1 development board manual, the on-board displays are common-cathode devices and are therefore active high:

docs.title: 3.2 Pin Constraints
docs.text:
The eight seven-segment displays on the EGO1 board are divided into left and right groups, each containing four digits:

  • The right group shares segment signals CA0~CG0 and DP0.
  • The left group shares segment signals CA1~CG1 and DP1.
  • Each of the eight digits also has an independent digit-select signal, corresponding to BIT1~BIT8.

Thus, the four digits within a group share the same set of segment-select signals. The independent digit-select signal determines which digit is currently illuminated.

The following tables organize the EGO1 pins related to the seven-segment displays by their labels.

docs.title: 3.2.1 Segment-Select Pins for the Two Groups
docs.text:
Segment Right-group label FPGA pin Left-group label FPGA pin a CA0 B4 CA1 D4 b CB0 A4 CB1 E3 c CC0 A3 CC1 D3 d CD0 B1 CD1 F4 e CE0 A1 CE1 F3 f CF0 B3 CF1 E2 g CG0 B2 CG1 D2 dp DP0 D5 DP1 H2

The four right-hand digits receive the same CA0~CG0, DP0 segment pattern, while the four left-hand digits receive the same CA1~CG1, DP1 pattern. Therefore, if several digit-select signals within one group are asserted simultaneously, all selected digits display the same content.

Important: The order of the segment-select signals must exactly match the segment order defined in your circuit and bit pattern. If your segment code uses {a, b, c, d, e, f, g, dp}, connect and assign the signals in CA/CB/CC/CD/CE/CF/CG/DP order. Mixing up the a~dp order illuminates the wrong segments.

docs.title: 3.2.2 Eight Digit-Select Signals
docs.text:
Name Display label FPGA pin DN0_K1 BIT1 G2 DN0_K2 BIT2 C2 DN0_K3 BIT3 C1 DN0_K4 BIT4 H1 DN1_K1 BIT5 G1 DN1_K2 BIT6 F1 DN1_K3 BIT7 E1 DN1_K4 BIT8 G6

The four right-hand digits correspond to BIT1~BIT4, and the four left-hand digits correspond to BIT5~BIT8. To illuminate only the rightmost digit in this exercise, assert BIT1.

Illuminating one digit requires two kinds of signals:

  1. Segment-select signals (which determine the glyph): A display has seven segments, a, b, c, d, e, f, g, plus the decimal point dp. For a common-cathode display, a high level (1) from the FPGA illuminates the corresponding segment.

  2. Digit-select signals (which determine the active position): Each of the eight digits has an independent select input. A digit displays the pattern currently present on its group's segment lines only when its digit-select signal is set to 1.

In short:

  • Segment select controls “what is displayed.”
  • Digit select controls “where it is displayed.”

For example, to display 5 on a digit in the right-hand group:

  1. Drive the segment code for 5 onto the right group's segment-select pins.
  2. Set the digit-select signal for the target digit to 1.

If the segment-select signals are set but no digit select is asserted, no digit lights. If multiple digit selects in one group are asserted simultaneously, those digits display the same glyph because they share the same segment-select signals.

docs.title: 3.3 Segment-Code Mapping (Truth Table)
docs.text:
Assume that the seven segments and decimal point are ordered from most significant bit to least significant bit as {a, b, c, d, e, f, g, dp}. To display 0, illuminate a, b, c, d, e, and f, while turning off g and dp. The segment code is therefore 8'b1111_1100.

Examples:

Displayed character Binary segment code {a,b,c,d,e,f,g} Hexadecimal 0 8'b1111_1100 8'hFC 1 8'b0110_0000 7'h60 2 8'b1101_1010 7'hDA 3 8'b1111_0010 7'hF2 ... ... ...

docs.title: 4. Laboratory Exercise: BCD-to-Seven-Segment Decoder
docs.text:
• Module name: bcd_to_7seg
  • Input: bcd_in (4-bit BCD code in the range 0–9)
  • Output 1: seg_out (7-bit segment-select output connected to a~g)
  • Output 2: ans_out (8-bit digit-select output connected to BIT1~BIT8)
  • Function: Use behavioral modeling with a case statement to convert a 4-bit BCD code into the corresponding seven-segment pattern. For an invalid input from 10 to 15, turn off all segments. Display the result on the rightmost digit of the EGO1 board.

docs.title: Step 1: Write the Design
docs.text:
Implement the decoding logic using always @(*) and a case statement.

Tip: In addition to assigning the segment-select output, remember to enable the digit-select signal for the first digit by setting it to 1.

docs.title: Step 2: Write the Testbench
docs.text: Use the for loop to generate input stimuli from 0 through 15. Inspect the waveform to determine whether the correct segment code is produced.

docs.title: Step 3: Assign Pins and Verify the Design on the Board
docs.text:
• Bind bcd_in to four slide switches on the EGO1 development board (see SW0~SW3 in the manual).
  • Bind the seven bits of seg_out to the corresponding segment pins of the right-hand display group (see CA0~CG0 in the manual).
  • Bind the eight bits of ans_out to the digit-select pins (see BIT8~BIT1 in the manual).
  • Synthesize the design, generate and download the bitstream, then toggle the switches and observe the displayed digit.

Question: What changes would you make to the code to display hexadecimal digits A–F in addition to 0–9?

docs.title: Appendix: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text: • Q: The code and pin assignments appear correct, but the rightmost display does not light. Why? A: Check that the segment-select signals are bound to the pins for the right-hand group and that the digit-select signal corresponding to the rightmost digit is set to 1.

docs.title: Digital Logic: Button Debouncing and Edge Detection
Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand mechanical button bounce and its effect on digital circuits.
  • Master counter-based button debouncing.
  • Master edge detection, which extracts a single pulse from a level signal.
  • Implement the correct behavior in which one button press increments a counter exactly once.

docs.title: 1.1 Physical Characteristics of a Mechanical Button
docs.text: The buttons on the development board are mechanical switches. When a button is pressed or released, its metal contacts bounce several times, causing the signal to switch rapidly between 0 and 1 for approximately 5–20 ms.

docs.title: 1.2 Effects of Bounce
docs.text:
If an unfiltered button signal directly drives a counter enable:

  • You expect one press to increment the counter by 1.
  • The counter may actually increment 3–10 times from one press.
  • Each bounce can produce an edge that triggers the count.

docs.title: 1.3 Experimental Observation
docs.text: As an initial experiment, connect the button directly to the counter enable without debouncing and observe the board. A single press may cause the number on the seven-segment display to jump by several counts. This is the direct effect of contact bounce.

docs.title: 2.1 Counter-Delay Debouncing Principle
docs.text:
The central idea is to sample the signal and wait for it to stabilize:

  1. Continuously sample the button level.
  2. When a level change is detected, start a delay counter.
  3. Count from zero. If the level changes again during the counting interval, the signal is still bouncing, so restart the count.
  4. If the counter reaches the configured limit—for example, the number of clock cycles corresponding to 20 ms—the level has remained stable and the output may be updated.

docs.title: 2.2 Calculating the Delay Parameter
docs.text:
• Target debounce interval: approximately 20 ms
  • System clock: 100 MHz → one cycle = 10 ns
  • 20 ms = 20,000,000 ns
  • Required count = 20,000,000 / 10 = 2,000,000

Therefore, CNT_WIDTH= 2_000_000.

docs.title: 2.3 Button-Debounce Module
docs.text:
module btn_debounce #(
    parameter CNT_MAX = 20_000_000,
    parameter CNT_WIDTH = 25
) (
    input clk,
    input rst_n,
    input btn_in,   // 带抖动的按键，低电平有效
    output reg  btn_out  // 1周期输出脉冲，1代表按键被按下
);

    reg [CNT_WIDTH-1:0] cnt_20ms; // counter for time window


    // 计数器逻辑：检测按键是否稳定保持低电平
    always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (rst_n == 1'b0)
            cnt_20ms <= 'b0;
        else if (btn_in == 1'b1) 
            // 如果在此期间按键变高，说明是释放或抖动，清零
            cnt_20ms <= 'b0;
        else if (cnt_20ms == CNT_MAX - 1'b1 && btn_in == 1'b0)
            // 计数达到设定阈值 (19_999_999)，保持该值不再累加
            cnt_20ms <= cnt_20ms; 
        else
            // 按键为低电平且未达阈值，继续累加
            cnt_20ms <= cnt_20ms + 1'b1; 
    end

    // 脉冲生成逻辑：在 19_999_999 这一刻产生单周期脉冲
    always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (rst_n == 1'b0)
            btn_out <= 1'b0;
        else if (cnt_20ms == CNT_MAX - 2'd2)
            // 当计数器为 19_999_998 时，下一个时钟沿 cnt_20ms 将变为 19_999_999
            // 此时拉高 btn_out，使其刚好在 19_999_999 期间保持为高电平
            btn_out <= 1'b1;
        else
            // 其他时刻全部拉低，保证只有 1 个周期的脉冲
            btn_out <= 1'b0;
    end

endmodule

The module operates as shown below:

Sequence of operation:

  1. The button is pressed and the signal begins to bounce.
  2. Each level change resets cnt to zero.
  3. Once the level stabilizes, cnt increments normally.
  4. When cnt reaches DEBOUNCE_MAX, btn_out is updated to the current stable level.

docs.title: 3.1 Why Is Edge Detection Necessary?
docs.text:
When first writing hardware code, it is easy to make the intuitive mistake of placing an ordinary signal directly in the edge-triggered sensitivity list of an always block:

Incorrect:

always @(posedge btn_out) begin
    cnt <= cnt + 1'b1;
    ...
end
// 这里的信号 'btn_out' 只是普通信号，例如按键按下，并没有被用作时钟或复位

This is incorrect because a chip contains a dedicated global clock-routing network that provides extremely low delay and reliable synchronization. Using posedge or negedge on an ordinary signal forces the synthesis tool to treat it as a clock. Ordinary routing does not meet the physical requirements of a clock network and can introduce glitches, cause serious timing failures, or even prevent successful synthesis and implementation.

Correct:

always @(posedge clk) begin
    if(pos_edge)
       cnt <= cnt + 1'b1;
       ...
end

Here, pos_edge is synchronous with clk. When a rising-edge event occurs on btn_out, pos_edge becomes 1 for exactly one clock cycle. This captures the transition while keeping the circuit safe and stable.

Why not use if(btn_out)? btn_out is a level signal. It may remain 1 for several seconds while a button is held. If it is used directly as an enable, the counter continues to increment for the entire press—once on every enabled clock cycle—rather than incrementing only once per press.

Edge detection converts a level signal into a single-cycle pulse, which is high for exactly one clock cycle at the instant of the press.

docs.title: 3.2 Edge-Detection Principle
docs.text:
Store the signal's value from the previous clock cycle in a register. Comparing the current value with the preceding value reveals an edge:

信号：   0 0 0 1 1 1 1 0 0
上一拍： x 0 0 0 1 1 1 1 0
上升沿：     0 0 1 0 0 0 0 0   （当前=1 且 上一拍=0）
下降沿：     0 0 0 0 0 0 1 0   （当前=0 且 上一拍=1）

docs.title: 3.3 Edge-Detection Module
docs.text:
module edge_detect (
    input      clk,
    input      rst_n,
    input      sig_in,       // 输入信号（通常接消抖后的 btn_out）
    output     pos_edge,     // 上升沿脉冲（单周期）
    output     neg_edge      // 下降沿脉冲（单周期）
);
    reg sig_d;  // 延迟一拍的信号

    always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (!rst_n)
            sig_d <= 1'b0;
        else
            sig_d <= sig_in;
    end

    assign pos_edge = sig_in & ~sig_d;  // 当前高，上一拍低 → 上升沿
    assign neg_edge = ~sig_in & sig_d;  // 当前低，上一拍高 → 下降沿
endmodule

Timing waveform:

clk:      _|‾|_|‾|_|‾|_|‾|_|‾|_|‾|_|‾|_
sig_in:   _____|‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾|__________
sig_d:    ________|‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾|_______
pos_edge: _____|‾|__________________________
neg_edge: ___________________|‾|__________

docs.title: 3.4 Combining Debouncing and Edge Detection
docs.text:
In practice, the two modules are usually connected in series:

btn_in(有抖动) → btn_debounce → btn_out(干净电平) → edge_detect → pos_edge(单脉冲)

docs.title: Exercise: Button-Controlled Counter
docs.text:
Requirement: Toggle the state of an LED once for each button press.

Test the design on the board using one of the five buttons on the right side of the EGO1 development board.

docs.title: Appendix: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text:
• Q: Why does the count still jump after debouncing? A: Check whether COUNT_MAX is sufficiently large. A 20 ms interval (2,000,000 cycles at 100 MHz) is recommended. If the value is too small, the output may be updated before the bouncing has ended.

  • Q: Why is there no response to the button? A: Check the button's pin constraint. Consult the EGO1 manual to determine whether the button is active-high or active-low. For an active-low button, invert the signal or use falling-edge detection.

docs.title: Digital Logic: Dataflow Modeling and FPGA Verification
Objectives
docs.text:
• Master Verilog dataflow modeling using the continuous assignment statement assign.
  • Learn to write a simple testbench for simulation and verification.
  • Understand the difference between dataflow modeling and structural modeling with gate-level primitives.
  • Master FPGA pin assignment and the on-board verification flow.

docs.title: 1.1 What Is Dataflow Modeling?
docs.text: Dataflow modeling describes the logical relationship between a circuit's inputs and outputs using continuous assignment statements (assign). It abstracts away the underlying gate-level structure and describes functionality directly with Boolean expressions or operators, making it suitable for combinational logic.

docs.title: 1.2 Continuous Assignment with assign
docs.text:
• Syntax: assign wire_signal = expression;
  • Characteristics:
  • The assignment target must be of type wire, not reg.
  • Whenever any variable on the right-hand side changes, the left-hand side is updated immediately, modeling the continuous response of combinational logic.
  • Multiple assign statements execute concurrently, regardless of their order in the source file.

docs.title: Operators Commonly Used in Dataflow Modeling
docs.text: Operator category Symbols Example Bitwise logic ~, &, |, ^ y = a & b; Logical !, &&, || y = a && b; Arithmetic +, -, *, / sum = a + b; Relational >, <, >=, <= gt = a > b; Equality ==, != eq = a == b; Conditional (ternary) ? : y = sel ? a : b; Concatenation {} {cout, sum} = a + b;

docs.title: Bitwise Versus Logical Operators
docs.text:
• Logical operators (!, &&, ||) always produce an effective output width of one bit (0 or 1). They are commonly used in conditions such as if and while.
  • Bitwise operators (~, &, |) operate independently on each bit. Their output width matches the operand width, so they are commonly used in combinational datapath logic.
a b a | b a || b a & b a && b ~a !a 2'b01 2'b10 2'b11 1'b1 2'b00 1'b1 2'b10 1'b0 2'b01 2'b11 2'b11 1'b1 2'b01 1'b1 2'b10 1'b0 2'b00 2'b01 2'b01 1'b1 2'b00 1'b0 2'b11 1'b1

docs.title: 1.4 Dataflow Example: Three-Input Majority Voter
docs.text:
Design a three-input majority voter whose output is 1 when at least two of its three inputs are 1.

The logic expression is F = ab + ac + bc. The design is:

// 3-input majority voter (数据流描述)
module majority_3 (
    input  a, b, c,
    output out
);
    assign out = (a & b) | (a & c) | (b & c);
endmodule

Note the operator-precedence order: () > ~ > & > |.

For example, the expression F = a(b‘+c) is written in Verilog as:

assign F = a & (~b | c);

docs.title: 2.1 Basic Testbench Structure
docs.text:
A testbench is a simulation environment for testing a design module. It has no input or output ports, instantiates the design under test, and generates stimulus signals.

  • Module definition: A testbench is a top-level module with no input or output ports.
  • Signal declarations: Declare inputs to the design under test as type reg so that the testbench can generate stimuli. Declare outputs from the design under test as type wire so that the responses can be monitored.
  • Instantiate the design under test: Instantiate the module with a suitable instance name, such as DUT, and connect signals declared in the testbench to the corresponding DUT ports.
  • Generate stimuli: Generate test vectors in an initial or always block, often using loops and delays. This laboratory uses only initial.
  • Monitor results: Print output using system tasks such as $display and $monitor, or inspect the waveform.

docs.title: 2.2 Testbench Template
docs.text:
The following is a testbench template for the majority_3 module:

`timescale 1ns/1ps

module tb_majority_3();
    // 声明信号（与待测模块端口对应）
    reg a, b, c;
    wire out;

    // 实例化被测模块
    majority_3 uut (
        .a(a),
        .b(b),
        .c(c),
        .out(out)
    );

    // 产生激励
    initial begin
        // 在这里给输入赋值
    end

    // 监控输出（可选）
    initial begin
        $monitor(...);
    end
endmodule

docs.title: 2.3 Common Ways to Generate Stimuli
docs.text:
• Direct assignment: Use # delays to change inputs sequentially.
initial begin
    a = 0; b = 0; c = 0; 
    #10;
    a = 0; b = 0; c = 1; 
    #10;
    a = 0; b = 1; c = 0; 
    #10;
  // ... 覆盖所有组合
    $finish;
end
  • Automatically enumerate values with a loop (appropriate for a small number of variables): Verilog provides several loop statements. Three common forms are shown below.

1. for loop (most common)

integer i;
initial begin
    for (i = 0; i < 8; i = i + 1) begin
        {a, b, c} = i;  // 拼接赋值，自动遍历 000~111
        #10;
    end
    $finish;
end

2. while loop

integer i;
initial begin
    i = 0;
    while (i < 8) begin
        {a, b, c} = i;
        #10;
        i = i + 1;
    end
    $finish;
end

3. repeat loop (a fixed number of iterations)

integer i;
initial begin
    i = 0;
    repeat(8) begin
        {a, b, c} = i;
        #10;
        i = i + 1;
    end
    $finish;
end

Note: repeat executes a fixed number of times and is usually used when no loop variable is needed. If counting is required, an additional variable is still necessary.

docs.title: 2.4 Common System Tasks (Simulation Only)
docs.text:
• $display("format string", variable1, variable2, ...); Prints information during simulation, similarly to C's printf. It prints once each time it executes.
  • $monitor("format string", variable1, variable2, ...); Continuously monitors variables and prints a line whenever any of them changes. It is usually placed in a separate initial block.
  • $finish; Ends the simulation, preventing an excessively long default simulation from making the waveform difficult to inspect.

Example:

initial begin
    $monitor("time=%t a=%b b=%b c=%b out=%b", $time, a, b, c, out);
end

docs.title: 2.5 Complete Testbench Example for majority_3
docs.text:
`timescale 1ns/1ps

module tb_majority_3();
    reg a, b, c;
    wire out;
    integer i;

    // 实例化被测模块
    majority_3 uut (
        .a(a),
        .b(b),
        .c(c),
        .out(out)
    );

    initial begin
        $monitor("time=%3d: a=%b b=%b c=%b => out=%b", $time, a, b, c, out);
        for (i = 0; i < 8; i = i + 1) begin
            {a, b, c} = i;
            #10;
        end
        $finish;
    end
endmodule

docs.title: 3.1 Review: Structural Modeling with Primitive Gates
docs.text:
Verilog provides built-in basic gate primitives such as and, or, and xor. Instantiating and connecting these gates is called structural modeling.

Example: Implementing the majority voter with gate primitives

module majority_3_gate (
    input a, b, c,
    output out
);
    wire w1, w2, w3;
    and (w1, a, b);
    and (w2, a, c);
    and (w3, b, c);
    or  (out, w1, w2, w3);
endmodule

docs.title: 3.2 Comparing Coding Styles
docs.text:
The following table compares the two styles using the majority voter as an example:

Dataflow modeling Structural modeling with primitives Direct expression Basic gate instantiation verilogassign out = (a & b) | (a & c) | (b & c); verilogwire w1, w2, w3;and (w1, a, b);and (w2, a, c);and (w3, b, c);or (out, w1, w2, w3); Intermediate signals in steps (same result) Gate order may be changed (same result) verilogwire and_ab, and_ac, and_bc;assign and_ab = a & b;assign and_ac = a & c;assign and_bc = b & c;assign out = and_ab | and_ac | and_bc; verilogwire w1, w2, w3;or (out, w1, w2, w3);and (w1, a, b);and (w2, a, c);and (w3, b, c);

docs.title: 3.3 Comparison
docs.text:
Characteristic Dataflow modeling (assign) Structural modeling (gate primitives) Abstraction level Higher; close to a logic expression Lower; close to transistor/gate-level connections Conciseness Concise; often a single expression Verbose; requires several gate instances Readability Good; directly expresses the function Lower; requires interpreting gate-level connections Design efficiency High; suitable for complex combinational logic Low; suitable only for simple or instructional examples Synthesis result Optimized by the synthesis tool Closely follows specified gates; controllable but inefficient Typical use Combinational logic in practical designs Instructional demonstrations and special custom gate structures

Conclusion: Practical designs use dataflow or behavioral modeling almost exclusively; behavioral modeling is introduced later. Gate-level primitives are mainly used for instruction or specialized custom requirements.

docs.title: 4.1 What Is Synthesis?
docs.text:
Synthesis converts hardware description language (HDL) code into a concrete logic circuit, such as a gate-level netlist. Vivado's synthesis tool analyzes Verilog code such as assign statements, infers the corresponding logic gates and connections, and produces a netlist mapped to FPGA resources such as lookup tables (LUTs) and flip-flops (FFs).

Purposes of synthesis:

  • Verify that the code is accepted by the synthesis tool and can produce actual hardware.
  • Inspect the synthesized schematic to understand the hardware corresponding to the code.
  • Analyze resource utilization and estimated timing, which are beyond the scope of this course at present.

docs.title: 4.2 How Do I View the Synthesized Schematic?
docs.text:
1. Click Run Synthesis.
  2. After synthesis completes successfully, click Open Synthesized Design.
  3. In the Schematic view, inspect the circuit made up of logic gates, LUTs, and flip-flops.
  4. Zoom in to inspect how input signals pass through logic elements to produce outputs.
  5. Combinational logic is usually implemented with LUTs (lookup tables).

docs.title: How Do I View a Module's Truth Table or Logic Expression?
docs.text:
• Click a LUT cell in the schematic, usually labeled LUT2, LUT3, and so on. Its LUT equation appears in the properties window. The LUT equation is the logic expression inferred by Vivado during synthesis. It may differ from the original assign statement but will be functionally equivalent.

By examining the schematic and LUT properties, you can verify that the synthesis result matches your expectations and develop a deeper understanding of how Verilog code maps onto FPGA hardware.

Note: The synthesized schematic represents logic mapping, not the final placement and routing. The circuit after placement and routing is more complex, but its logical function remains unchanged.

docs.title: 5. Pin Assignment and On-Board Implementation in Vivado
docs.text: Note: Run synthesis before assigning pins.

docs.title: Method 1: Use the Vivado GUI (I/O Planning)
docs.text:
1. Click Run Synthesis.
  2. After synthesis completes, click Open Synthesized Design.
  3. Click I/O Planning in Vivado's top toolbar, or select Layout → I/O Planning.
  4. The I/O Ports window lists all top-level ports.
  5. In the Package Pin column, double-click the cell for a port and enter its physical pin identifier.
  6. In the I/O Std column, select LVCMOS33, according to the board voltage.
  7. Save the constraints with File → Save Constraints. Select or create an XDC file to store the current assignments.
  8. You can also generate the constraint file by clicking Write XDC in the toolbar.

Tip: Consult the development board schematic or official documentation for pin identifiers. Documentation for the EGO1 board is available under References on the course Blackboard site. If a pin identifier is unavailable after you enter it, confirm that the correct FPGA part was selected when the project was created.

docs.title: Method 2: Write the XDC File Manually (Review)
docs.text:
Add a new constraint file, xxx.xdc, to the project, then enter and edit the following content. The order of the constraints does not affect their behavior.

Example XDC file: Replace each question mark with the correct pin for the board.

## 输入引脚 (拨码开关) 
set_property PACKAGE_PIN ?? [get_ports {a}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {a}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN ?? [get_ports {b}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {b}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN ?? [get_ports {c}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {c}]

## 输出引脚 (LED)
set_property PACKAGE_PIN ?? [get_ports {out}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {out}]

Reference: Consult the EGO1 board manual or the pin labels printed next to the peripherals. If a pin identifier is not listed in the graphical interface, confirm that the project uses the correct FPGA part.

docs.title: 4.2 Implementation and Bitstream Generation
docs.text:
• Click Run Implementation to perform placement and routing. After implementation completes, you can inspect the timing report.
  • Click Generate Bitstream to generate the .bit file. Vivado displays a completion dialog when generation succeeds.
  • You may also click Generate Bitstream directly. Vivado then runs Synthesis, Implementation, and Generate Bitstream automatically without requiring intervention between stages.

docs.title: 4.3 Programming the FPGA Development Board
docs.text:
1. Connect and power on the board, ensuring that the programming cable, such as USB-JTAG, is connected.
  2. Click Open Hardware Manager → Auto Connect. Vivado automatically detects the board.
  3. Select Program Device in the Hardware window.
  4. Confirm that the bitstream path in the dialog is correct, then click Program.
  5. After programming completes, toggle the switches and verify that the LED follows the majority-voter logic.

docs.title: Exercise: Implement a Full Adder with Dataflow Modeling (assign)
docs.text:
• Module name: FullAdder

  • Inputs: a, b, cin

  • Outputs: s, cout

  • Function: As shown in the circuit diagram.

  • Requirement: Use assign statements and operators.

docs.title: Step 1: Write the Design
docs.text:
• Derive the expressions for cout and s.
  • Implement the design with assign statements.

docs.title: Step 2: Write and Verify the Testbench
docs.text:
• Draw the circuit's truth table on paper.
  • Compare it with the simulation result. You may either compare the log produced by $monitor or inspect the waveform directly.

docs.title: Step 3: Synthesize
docs.text: • Click Run Synthesis in Vivado and wait for synthesis to complete. If an error occurs, correct the code according to the diagnostic message.

docs.title: Step 4: Assign Pins
docs.text:
• Add pin constraints to the Exercise 1 design. For example, connect a/b/cin to three slide switches and s/cout to LEDs.
  • Create the constraints either by editing an XDC file or by using the I/O Planning graphical interface.

docs.title: Step 5: Generate the Bitstream and Verify on the Board
docs.text: • Click Generate Bitstream, program the development board with the resulting bitstream, and verify the design's function.

docs.title: Appendix: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text:
• Q: Can the left-hand side of an assign statement be type reg? A: No. It must be wire or a related net type such as tri.
  • Q: Why is the simulation waveform a straight line? A: Check whether the testbench contains $finish or whether the simulation interval is too long. Use Zoom Fit and Zoom In to display a suitable portion of the waveform.
  • Q: Why is the LED off or unresponsive after the board is programmed? A: Check the pin constraints, confirm that programming succeeded, and verify that the development board is powered on.
  • Q: Why can I not find the ports in I/O Planning? A: You must run Synthesis and open the synthesized design before the list of I/O ports is available.

docs.title: Digital Logic: Chasing LEDs and Multiplexed Seven-Segment Displays
Objectives
docs.text:
• Learn to implement a chasing-LED effect with a shift register.
  • Understand the principle of multiplexed scanning for multi-digit seven-segment displays.
  • Implement an eight-LED chasing pattern and a four-digit display on the EGO1 development board.

docs.title: 1.1 Design Objective
docs.text:
Implement a chasing pattern on eight EGO1 LEDs (LED0–LED7):

  • Exactly one LED is on at any time.
  • The illuminated position moves once per second.
  • It moves from left (LED7) to right (LED0).
  • After reaching the rightmost position, it returns to the leftmost position and repeats.

docs.title: 1.2 Design Approach
docs.text:
The chasing-LED circuit consists of a clock divider plus a circular shift:

  1. Use the counter to divide the 100 MHz clock down to 1 Hz.
  2. Whenever the counter reaches one second, circularly shift the LED pattern one position to the right.

A circular right shift can be implemented with the Verilog concatenation operator:

led <= {led[0], led[7:1]};  // 循环右移

What does this statement do?

  • led[7:1]: Select the upper seven bits.
  • led[0]: Select the least-significant bit.
  • {led[0], led[7:1]}: Concatenate the least-significant bit in front of the upper seven bits, shifting the entire pattern one position to the right.

Starting from led = 8'b1000_0000, where only LED7 is on, the pattern is:

8'b1000_0000  →  8'b0100_0000  →  8'b0010_0000  →  ...  →  8'b0000_0001  →  8'b1000_0000
   LED7亮          LED6亮           LED5亮                     LED0亮          回到LED7

docs.title: 1.3 Initialization
docs.text:
On a Xilinx FPGA, registers are automatically initialized at power-up to the initial values specified in the source code. We can therefore use an initial statement to set the initial state without a reset signal:

reg [31:0] cnt = 0;          // 计数器初始为 0
initial led = 8'b1000_0000;  // LED 初始状态：最左边亮

Note: Xilinx FPGA synthesis supports initial statements, but not all FPGA vendors do. This course uses the EGO1 development board with a Xilinx Artix-7 FPGA, so this construct is supported.

docs.title: 1.4 Parameterized Division Factor
docs.text:
Here, a parameter specifies the division factor so that it is easy to switch between simulation and on-board operation:

module running_led #(
    parameter MAX_COUNT = 100_000_000  // 默认：100MHz / 1亿 = 1Hz
)(
    input            clk,
    output reg [7:0] led
);

Pass a smaller value during simulation to accelerate it:

running_led #(.MAX_COUNT(10)) uut ( ... );  // 仿真用，10 个周期移一位

Use the default value of 100 million on the board; the design source does not need to be modified.

docs.title: 1.5 Complete Design
docs.text:
module running_led #(
    parameter MAX_COUNT = 100_000_000
)(
    input            clk,
    output reg [7:0] led
);

    reg [31:0] cnt = 0;

    initial led = 8'b1000_0000;

    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (cnt == MAX_COUNT - 1) begin
            cnt <= 0;
            led <= {led[0], led[7:1]};
        end else begin
            cnt <= cnt + 1;
        end
    end

endmodule

Key points:

  • Counter cnt counts from 0 through MAX_COUNT - 1. At the terminal count, it returns to zero and shifts the LED pattern.
  • Counting and shifting occur in the same always block, keeping the logic clear.

docs.title: 1.6 Testbench
docs.text:
`timescale 1ns/1ps

module tb_running_led();
    reg        clk;
    wire [7:0] led;

    running_led #(.MAX_COUNT(10)) uut (
        .clk(clk),
        .led(led)
    );

    initial clk = 0;
    always #5 clk = ~clk;  // 100MHz

    initial begin
        #2000;
        $finish;
    end
endmodule

In the simulation waveform, led should shift right once every ten clock cycles (100 ns), progressing from 8'b1000_0000 to 8'b0100_0000, 8'b0010_0000, and so on.

The simulation waveform is shown below:

docs.title: 1.8 On-Board Verification
docs.text:
1. Create a project in Vivado and add running_led.v and the constraint file.
  2. Run synthesis → implementation → bitstream generation → programming.
  3. Verify that the eight LEDs illuminate in sequence from left to right, moving one position per second.

docs.title: 2.1 Why Is Multiplexed Scanning Necessary?
docs.text:
Recall that each of the EGO1's left and right groups shares one set of segment-select signals. At any instant, all digits in a group can therefore show only the same glyph.

How can they display different content? The answer is multiplexed scanning, or time-division multiplexing.

docs.title: 2.2 Multiplexed Scanning
docs.text:
1. Illuminate only one digit for a very short interval and display its corresponding value.
  2. Switch to the next digit.
  3. Alternate rapidly among the four digits.
  4. If switching is sufficiently fast (>200 Hz per digit), persistence of vision makes the digits appear to be illuminated simultaneously.

Timing diagram:

时间 →
BIT1: ████                    ████                    ████
BIT2:      ████                    ████                    ████
BIT3:           ████                    ████                    ████
BIT4:                ████                    ████                    
段码:  D0   D1   D2   D3   D0   D1   D2   D3   ...

docs.title: 2.3 Implementation Architecture
docs.text: The following diagram shows a general architecture. Clock division and counting produce a slow display clock (DISP_CLK) and digit-select decoding signals B1B0. These determine which digit is illuminated at a given time and which pattern it displays.

docs.title: 2.4 Clock Divider
docs.text:
The following parameter values may be used as references:

parameter PERIOD = 200_000;   // 500Hz，显示稳定
// parameter PERIOD = 250_000; // 400Hz，显示稳定
// parameter PERIOD = 5_000_000; // 20Hz，能明显看到一位一位轮流亮
// parameter PERIOD = 2_500_000; // 40Hz，会有明显闪烁
// parameter PERIOD = 1_000_000; // 100Hz，轻微闪烁

reg [31:0] div_cnt;
reg        scan_clk;

always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n) begin
        div_cnt  <= 32'd0;
        scan_clk <= 1'b0;
    end else if (div_cnt == (PERIOD >> 1) - 1) begin
        div_cnt  <= 32'd0;
        scan_clk <= ~scan_clk;
    end else begin
        div_cnt  <= div_cnt + 1'd1;
    end
end

Key points:

  • PERIOD is the number of system-clock cycles in one period of scan_clk.
  • When the counter reaches half of a period, scan_clk toggles.
  • This produces a stable, low-frequency scan clock.

docs.title: 2.5 Scan Counter
docs.text:
reg [1:0] scan_cnt;

always @(posedge scan_clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n)
        scan_cnt <= 2'd0;
    else if (scan_cnt == 2'd3)
        scan_cnt <= 2'd0;
    else
        scan_cnt <= scan_cnt + 1'd1;
end

The counter values have a direct interpretation:

  • 0: Scan Digit 1.
  • 1: Scan Digit 2.
  • 2: Scan Digit 3.
  • 3: Scan Digit 4.

docs.title: 2.6 Digit-Select Signals
docs.text:
Use one-hot encoding so that only one digit is selected at any time. The following order is only an example:

scan_cnt Selected digit 2'd0 BIT1 (leftmost) 2'd1 BIT2 2'd2 BIT3 2'd3 BIT4 (rightmost)

docs.title: 2.7 Segment-Select Signals
docs.text: The EGO1 uses common-cathode displays, so a high level illuminates a segment. The segment-code format is seg = {a, b, c, d, e, f, g, dp}:

docs.title: 3.1 Design Objective
docs.text: Display 1234 on either the left or right group of four seven-segment digits on the EGO1.

docs.title: 3.2 Code Framework
docs.text:
Complete the sections marked ______ in the following code:

module dynamic_display #(
    parameter PERIOD = 200_000   // 500Hz，显示稳定
)(
    input        clk,        // 系统时钟 100MHz
    input        rst_n,      // 低电平有效
    input  [3:0] digit0,     
    input  [3:0] digit1,      
    input  [3:0] digit2,      
    input  [3:0] digit3,      
    output reg [7:0] seg,    // 段选输出 {a,b,c,d,e,f,g,dp}
    output reg [3:0] an      // 片选输出 BIT1~BIT4 或者 BIT5~BIT8
);

    reg [31:0] div_cnt;
    reg        scan_clk;
    reg [1:0]  scan_cnt;

    // -------- 分频器 --------
    always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (!rst_n) begin
            div_cnt  <= 32'd0;
            scan_clk <= 1'b0;
        end else if (div_cnt == _____________) begin
            div_cnt  <= 32'd0;
            scan_clk <= _____________;
        end else begin
            div_cnt  <= _____________;
        end
    end

    // -------- 扫描计数器 --------
    always @(posedge scan_clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (!rst_n)
            scan_cnt <= 2'd0;
        else if (_____________)
            scan_cnt <= 2'd0;
        else
            scan_cnt <= _____________;
    end

    // -------- 数据选择 + 片选 --------
    reg [3:0] bcd_data;

    always @(*) begin
        case (scan_cnt)
            2'd0: begin bcd_data = digit0; an = _____________; end
            2'd1: begin bcd_data = digit1; an = _____________; end
            2'd2: begin bcd_data = digit2; an = _____________; end
            2'd3: begin bcd_data = digit3; an = _____________; end
            default: begin bcd_data = 4'd0; an = _____________; end
        endcase
    end

    // -------- 七段译码 --------
    always @(*) begin
        case (bcd_data)
            4'd0: seg[7:0] = _____________;
            4'd1: seg[7:0] = _____________;
            4'd2: seg[7:0] = _____________;
            4'd3: seg[7:0] = _____________;
            4'd4: seg[7:0] = _____________;
            4'd5: seg[7:0] = _____________;
            ..._____________
            default: seg[7:0] = 7'b00000000;
        endcase
    end

endmodule

docs.title: 4. Laboratory Exercise
docs.text:
Complete the fill-in-the-blank code in Demo 2. Add the following module at the beginning of the source file (creating a new file is recommended), set display as the top-level module, add an XDC file, and assign the pins. Display 1234 on four EGO1 seven-segment digits.

module display (
    input        clk,
    input        rst_n,
    output [7:0] seg, //段选信号
    output [3:0] an //片选信号
);
    dynamic_display u_disp (
        .clk(clk), .rst_n(rst_n),
        .digit0(4'd1), .digit1(4'd2),
        .digit2(4'd3), .digit3(4'd4),
        .seg(seg), .an(an)
    );
endmodule

docs.title: Appendix: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text:
• Q: Why does the display flicker, or why are some digits off? A: Check that the digit-select signal an uses one-hot encoding, with only one active bit at a time, and that scan_cnt covers all four digits.

  • Q: Why does the display show incorrect glyphs? A: Check that the bit order of seg, {a,b,c,d,e,f,g,dp}, matches the relationship between seg[7]~seg[0] and the pin constraints. Verify each bit against the glyph diagram in Section 2.7.

  • Q: Why is only one digit illuminated? A: Check that scan_cnt is counting correctly in the simulation waveform and that the digit-select pins are constrained correctly.

docs.title: Digital Logic: Environment Setup and Engineering Practice
Objectives
docs.text:
• Become familiar with the laboratory platform used in this course: the EDA tool and FPGA development board.
  • Understand the key requirements for installing and configuring Vivado.
  • Become familiar with the hardware components and basic architecture of the EGO1 development board.
  • Master the complete Vivado project development flow: creating a project, adding files, functional simulation, synthesis and implementation, bitstream generation, and on-board verification.
  • Understand the basic principles of FPGAs and how they differ from conventional CPUs.

docs.title: 1. Experimental Platform
docs.text: This course uses a combination of an EDA tool and an FPGA development board for hardware experiments.

docs.title: 1.1 EDA Tool: Vivado 2018.3
docs.text:
• Purpose: Vivado is the development environment designed by Xilinx for its FPGA products. It enables developers to synthesize (compile) hardware designs, perform timing analysis, inspect RTL schematics, simulate circuit responses to different stimuli, and configure target devices through a programmer.
  • Version: This course standardizes on Vivado 2018.3.

docs.title: 1.2 FPGA Development Board: EGO1
docs.text:
• Main device: A Xilinx Artix-7 FPGA, part number xc7a35tcsg324-1.

  • Main on-board peripherals:

  • Power switch

  • Potentiometer
  • Five push buttons
  • Sixteen slide switches
  • Reset button
  • Eight seven-segment displays
  • Sixteen LEDs
  • Other interfaces: VGA, audio, USB-UART/JTAG (for connecting the board to a computer and programming it), and USB-PS/2

docs.title: 2.1 Important Notes
docs.text:
Vivado requires substantial disk space and imposes strict requirements on paths. Observe the following points:

  • Disk space: Reserve at least 20 GB of free space on the target drive.
  • Path naming: The operating-system username, the folder containing the installation package, and the final Vivado installation path must not contain Chinese characters or spaces.
  • Download link: Refer to 'resources' on top of the website.
  • Installer and license: Download the installer archive Xilinx_Vivado_SDK_2018.3_1207_2324.tar.gz and the license archive Vivado2018.3_licence.zip, then extract both archives.
  • Edition: Select Vivado HL Design Edition in the installer.
  • Custom installation (to save space): On the component-selection screen, it is strongly recommended that you select only the components required for this course:
  • Expand 7 Series devices and select only Artix-7. Clear the selections for other devices such as Kintex-7 and Spartan-7.
  • Import the license: After installation, open Vivado License Manager, select Load License -> Copy License..., and import the downloaded .lic file.

docs.title: 2.2 Installation Procedure
docs.text:
• Extract the installer package and double-click xsetup.exe:
  • Skip the software update and click Continue:
  • On this screen, select I Agree:
  • Select the second option, Vivado HL Design Edition:
  • To save disk space, select only the component required for this course, Artix-7:
  • You may change the installation directory. Ensure that its path contains no Chinese characters, then click Next:
  • After installation, open the license manager and click Load License -> Copy License:
  • Locate the license file and click Open:
  • Click View License Status to inspect the license status:
  • Double-click the desktop shortcut to start Vivado.

docs.title: 3. Standard Vivado Project Development Flow
docs.text: The complete flow for hardware verification with Vivado and an FPGA development board consists of the following six steps:

docs.title: Step 1: Create or Open a Vivado Project
docs.text:
• Start Vivado. On the start screen, click Create Project; alternatively, select File -> Create Project in the upper-left corner.
  • Set the project name and path. Neither the project name nor its file path may contain Chinese characters or spaces.

Create project subdirectory: This option is selected by default. It creates a subfolder with the project name under the specified path.

  • Select RTL Project as the project type.

  • The next screens add source and constraint files. Click Next to skip them for now; the files will be created separately later.

  • Under Default Part, search for and select the device used on the EGO1 development board: xc7a35tcsg324-1.

docs.title: Step 2: Add or Create Source Files
docs.text:
• Three types of files must be added to the project: design sources, simulation sources, and constraints.
  • They can be added while creating the project (this method is not used here) or after the project has been created by clicking Add Sources (or the + icon).
  • Create a circuit design file (Design Source) named lab1_design.v. Enter lab1_design in File name.
  • Keep the default options, then click Finish -> OK.
  • The design file has now been created. The project view and the initial contents displayed after double-clicking the source file are shown below.
  • Complete the source file and save it.
module lab1_design(
    input [7:0] sw,
    output [7:0] led
);
    assign led = sw;
endmodule
  • In the same way, create the simulation file (Simulation Source) lab1_sim.v. Complete the simulation code and save it.
`timescale 1ns / 1ps

module lab1_sim( );

    reg [7:0] tb_sw = 8'h0000;
    wire [7:0] tb_led;

    lab1_design dut(
    .sw(tb_sw),
    .led(tb_led)
    );

    always #10 tb_sw=tb_sw + 1'b1;
endmodule
  • Create the constraint file (Constrain Source) lab1.xdc.
  • Enter the following pin constraints:
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {led[7]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {led[6]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {led[5]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {led[4]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {led[3]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {led[2]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {led[1]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {led[0]}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN F6 [get_ports {led[7]}]
set_property PACKAGE_PIN G4 [get_ports {led[6]}]
set_property PACKAGE_PIN G3 [get_ports {led[5]}]
set_property PACKAGE_PIN J4 [get_ports {led[4]}]
set_property PACKAGE_PIN H4 [get_ports {led[3]}]
set_property PACKAGE_PIN J3 [get_ports {led[2]}]
set_property PACKAGE_PIN J2 [get_ports {led[1]}]
set_property PACKAGE_PIN K2 [get_ports {led[0]}]

set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {sw[7]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {sw[6]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {sw[5]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {sw[4]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {sw[3]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {sw[2]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {sw[1]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {sw[0]}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN P5 [get_ports {sw[7]}]
set_property PACKAGE_PIN P4 [get_ports {sw[6]}]
set_property PACKAGE_PIN P3 [get_ports {sw[5]}]
set_property PACKAGE_PIN P2 [get_ports {sw[4]}]
set_property PACKAGE_PIN R2 [get_ports {sw[3]}]
set_property PACKAGE_PIN M4 [get_ports {sw[2]}]
set_property PACKAGE_PIN N4 [get_ports {sw[1]}]
set_property PACKAGE_PIN R1 [get_ports {sw[0]}]
  • Pin constraints consist of IOSTANDARD settings and PIN assignments. Set the IOSTANDARD of every port to LVCMOS33. The corresponding pins (PIN) can be found in Ego1_UserManual_v2.2.pdf or printed next to the associated peripherals on the development board.

docs.title: Step 3: Run Functional Simulation
docs.text:
• In the Flow Navigator on the left, click Run Simulation.
  • Vivado generates a waveform that records the states of the circuit's input and output signals.
  • Important: Inspect the waveform carefully to verify the circuit's function. If the logic is incorrect, modify the design file and rerun the simulation. Proceed to on-board implementation only after the functional simulation passes. You may also experiment with the following controls and learn what each one does.

docs.title: Step 4: Synthesize, Implement, and Generate the Bitstream
docs.text:
After confirming correct functionality, perform the following operations in order to convert the code into a hardware netlist:

  1. Click Run Synthesis.
  2. Click Run Implementation.
  3. Click Generate Bitstream to generate the final .bit file used to program the board.

Important: If any Error or Critical Warning occurs during these steps, inspect and correct the project settings, design code, or constraint file before generating the bitstream again.

docs.title: Step 5: Connect the Development Board
docs.text:
• Connect the computer to the USB-UART/JTAG port on the EGO1 development board using a data cable.
  • Turn on the EGO1 development board.
  • In Vivado, click Open Hardware Manager, followed by Open Target -> Auto Connect.
  • If the connection succeeds, the target device xc7a35t_0 appears in the Hardware window.

docs.title: Step 6: Program the Device and Verify It on the Board
docs.text:
• In Hardware Manager, click Program Device, select the newly generated .bit file, and click Program.
  • When programming is complete, the "Done" LED on the EGO1 board lights up, indicating that the circuit has been successfully implemented on the FPGA.
  • Toggle the input switches and observe the outputs to verify that the hardware behaves as designed.

docs.title: 4. Disconnecting the Hardware and Reconfiguring the Device
4.1 Safe Disconnection
docs.text:
At the end of the laboratory session, it is strongly recommended that you disconnect the development board in the following order. Never hot-plug the board while it is powered:

  1. Disconnect the software connection: Enter disconnect_hw_server in the Tcl Console at the bottom of Vivado and press Enter to disconnect Vivado from the FPGA.
  2. Disconnect the hardware: Turn off the EGO1 development board before unplugging the USB cable.

docs.title: 4.2 Changing the FPGA Device in a Project
docs.text:
If you selected the wrong device when creating the project, use the following steps to change it:

  • Under PROJECT MANAGER in the Flow Navigator, click Settings.

  • Select General, then click the ... button next to Project device to open the device selector.

  • Search for and select xc7a35tcsg324-1, then click OK.

  • Click Apply at the bottom of the Settings window to apply the configuration.

  • Close the Vivado project. In the project directory, delete the entire xxx.runs directory. This removes temporary files containing information about the previous device so that the change takes effect. Then restart Vivado.

docs.title: 5. Laboratory Exercise
docs.text:
1. Follow the development flow in this tutorial to implement and verify a simple switch-controlled LED circuit on the EGO1 development board.

  2. Input: Eight slide switches (sw[7:0])

  3. Output: Eight LEDs (led[7:0])
  4. Function: The position of each switch directly controls whether the corresponding LED is on or off.

  5. Check-off requirement: Reproduce the simulation waveform and demonstrate the circuit on the board.

  6. To support later exercises, you may download and install Vivado 2018.3 on your personal computer (optional).

Vivado supports only Windows and Linux. Download the Linux installer from the AMD website.

Running Vivado on macOS requires a virtual machine.

docs.title: Digital Logic: Memory and IP Cores
Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand the fundamental concepts and operation of memory.
  • Master the design of a single-port RAM in Verilog.
  • Learn to use the Vivado Block RAM IP core to design efficient memory.

docs.title: 1. Memory Fundamentals
docs.text:
Characteristic RAM (Random Access Memory) ROM (Read-Only Memory) Full name Random Access Memory Read-Only Memory Access Read and write Read only

On an FPGA, we primarily use Block RAM, a hardware resource within the FPGA that provides high bandwidth and low latency.

As shown below, a memory is accessed through addr.

If a memory has K address bits and each storage location is N bits wide, its capacity is N × 2^K bits.

docs.title: 2. Verilog Implementation: Single-Port RAM
docs.text: A single-port RAM can perform only one operation at a time—either a read or a write—but has the lowest cost.

docs.title: 2.1 Asynchronous Read
docs.text:
The read path is combinational, so data is available immediately.

module ram_single_port #(
    parameter ADDR_WIDTH = 10,  // 地址宽度（2^10 = 1024个单元）
    parameter DATA_WIDTH = 8   // 数据宽度（8位）
) (
    input  clk,
    input  we,                      // 写使能（高电平写入）
    input  [ADDR_WIDTH-1:0] addr,   // 地址
    input  [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] din,    // 数据输入
    output [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] dout    // 数据输出
);

    // 声明存储体：1024×8 的 RAM
    reg [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] mem [0:(1<<ADDR_WIDTH)-1];

    // 同步读写
    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (we)
            mem[addr] <= din;  // 写入
    end

    // 异步读出（组合逻辑）
    assign dout = mem[addr];

endmodule

Key points:

  • reg [7:0] mem [0:1023] defines 1024 storage locations of eight bits each.
  • mem[addr] <= din performs the write on the rising edge of the clock.
  • dout = mem[addr] is a combinational read with no clock-cycle latency.

docs.title: 2.2 Synchronous Read
docs.text:
The read path is sequential and has a one-cycle latency. Place the read logic in an always block and use a non-blocking assignment:

module ram_sync_read #(
    parameter ADDR_WIDTH = 10,
    parameter DATA_WIDTH = 8
) (
    input  clk,
    input  we,
    input  [ADDR_WIDTH-1:0] addr,
    input  [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] din,
    output reg [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] dout
);

    reg [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] mem [0:(1<<ADDR_WIDTH)-1];

    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (we)
            mem[addr] <= din;
        else
            dout <= mem[addr];  // 同步读出
    end

endmodule

Key points:

  • dout <= mem[addr]: The read is sequential and captures data on a rising edge of the clock.
  • Advantage: It integrates naturally with sequential designs and supports pipelining.

docs.title: 2.3 Initializing RAM for ROM-Like Operation
docs.text:
Sometimes a RAM must already contain data at power-up, such as program code or a lookup table:

module ram_with_init #(
    parameter DATA_WIDTH = 10,
    parameter ADDR_WIDTH = 8
) (
    input  clk,
    input  we,
    input  [ADDR_WIDTH-1:0] addr,
    input  [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] din,
    output [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] dout
);

    reg [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] mem [0:(1<<ADDR_WIDTH)-1];

    // 从文件初始化
    initial begin
        $readmemh("mem_init.hex", mem);  // 从 .hex 文件读取数据
    end

    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (we)
            mem[addr] <= din;
    end

    assign dout = mem[addr];

endmodule

.hex file format (hexadecimal):

3C  // 地址 0
10  // 地址 1
A5  // 地址 2
FF  // 地址 3
...

docs.title: 3.1 Why Use an IP Core?
docs.text:
A RAM written manually in Verilog may not make optimal use of the FPGA's physical Block RAM resources during synthesis. Vivado's Block RAM IP core provides:

  • Automatic optimization to use FPGA Block RAM resources efficiently.
  • Multiple configuration options, including width, depth, and initial values.
  • Better performance and lower resource use than a manually written RTL implementation.

docs.title: 3.2 Creating a Block RAM IP Core
docs.text:
Step 1: Open the IP Catalog

In Vivado, select Project Manager → IP Catalog.

Step 2: Search for Block RAM

Enter Block Memory Generator in the search box and select the official Xilinx IP.

Step 3: Configure the Parameters

Open the IP Customization dialog and configure it as shown in the following figures.

Step 4: Generate the IP Core

  1. Click OK to finish the configuration.
  2. Vivado generates the RTL and simulation files.
  3. The IP core appears in the project's ip_repo.

docs.title: 3.3 Block RAM IP Interface
docs.text:
The generated Block RAM IP core has the following ports for a single-port configuration:

module blk_mem_gen_0 (
    input  clka,           // 时钟
    input  wea,            // 写使能（[0] 对应字节使能）
    input  [9:0] addra,    // 地址
    input  [7:0] dina,     // 数据输入
    output [7:0] douta     // 数据输出
);

docs.title: Instantiating the Block RAM IP in a Design
docs.text:
module ram_controller (
    input  clk,
    input  we,
    input  [9:0] addr,
    input  [7:0] din,
    output [7:0] dout
);

    // 调用生成的 IP 核
    blk_mem_gen_0 ram_inst (
        .clka(clk),
        .wea(we),  
        .addra(addr),
        .dina(din),
        .douta(dout)
    );

endmodule

docs.title: 4.1 Requirements
docs.text:
Design and verify a basic RAM module with the following behavior:

  • Capacity: 1024 × 8 bits (10 address bits and 8 data bits)
  • Operations: Synchronous read and synchronous write
  • Test: Write several values to different addresses, then read them back and verify them

docs.title: 4.2 RAM Module Implementation
docs.text:
Design description:

  • addr is 10 bits wide and addresses 2^10 = 1024 locations.
  • A high we performs a write; a low we performs a read.
  • Both reads and writes occur on a rising edge of the clock. The read output becomes valid on the rising edge after a stable address has been applied.
  • The design may be implemented either in Verilog or with the IP core.

docs.title: 4.3 Simulation Test
docs.text:
Testbench procedure:

  1. Write phase: Write test data to several addresses.
  2. Read phase: Read the previously written addresses and verify the returned data.

  • Practice assembling the independent modules into a complete system.
  • Understand module-interface design and signal-naming conventions.
  • Build a single-digit hexadecimal counter display: each button press advances the display by one value in a repeating 0–F–0 sequence.

docs.title: 1.1 Required Modules
docs.text:
In previous weeks, we implemented the following independent modules:

Module Function counter_mod Modulo-N counter with enable and carry dynamic_display Seven-segment display driver btn_debounce Button debouncing edge_detect Edge detection

docs.title: 2.1 Functional Description
docs.text:
Design a single-digit hexadecimal counter display:

  • Use one seven-segment digit to display a single hexadecimal value.
  • Display sequence: 0 → 1 → 2 → ... → 9 → A → B → ... → F → 0, repeating continuously.
  • Increment the displayed value by 1 on each button press.
  • Button debouncing ensures that each press produces exactly one pulse.
  • Pressing the reset button clears the value to zero.

docs.title: 2.2 Module Decomposition
docs.text: Submodule Instances Function counter_mod #(.MOD(16)) 1 Modulo-16 counter (0–9, A–F) dynamic_display 1 Display driver using one digit btn_debounce 1 Button debouncing edge_detect 1 Button edge detection

docs.title: 2.3 Design Flow
docs.text:
按键 → 消抖 → 边沿检测 → 计数器enable → 计数器输出 → 数码管显示
(btn)  (clean) (pulse)    (en)         (count)      (seg)

docs.title: 3.1 Port Declarations
docs.text:
module hex_counter_top (
    input        clk,       // 100MHz 系统时钟
    input        btn,       // 按键 （Ego1：R15）
    output [7:0] seg,       // 数码管段选
    output [3:0] an         // 数码管片选
);

docs.title: 3.2 Complete Top-Level Module Framework
docs.text:
module hex_counter_top (
    input        clk,       // 100MHz 系统时钟
    input        btn_inc,   // 增加按键
    output [7:0] seg,       // 数码管段选
    output [3:0] an         // 数码管片选
);

    // 内部信号
    wire btn_clean; //消抖后的按键信号
    wire btn_pulse; //按键脉冲
    wire [3:0] count;

    // 按键消抖
    btn_debounce u_deb (
        .clk(clk), .rst_n(1'b1),
        .btn_in(btn), .btn_out(btn_clean)
    );

    // 边沿检测
    edge_detect u_edge (
        .clk(clk), .rst_n(1'b1),
        .sig_in(btn_clean),
        .pos_edge(btn_pulse), .neg_edge()
    );

    // 计数器
    counter_mod ...

    // 数码管显示
    dynamic_display ...

endmodule

docs.title: 3.3 Key Connections
docs.text: Signal Source Destination Purpose btn → btn_clean Button → debounce module Debounced signal Remove button bounce btn_clean → btn_pulse Debounce → edge detector Pulse signal Trigger on the rising edge btn_pulse → counter_mod.en Pulse → counter Count enable Increment once per pulse count → digit[?] Counter → display Single-digit value Hexadecimal display digit[?] 0 Display Other digits remain blank seg, an Display driver External display Segment- and digit-select signals

docs.title: Step 1: Prepare the Submodules
docs.text:
Copy the following modules into the project:

  • counter_mod.v —check the parameter setting
  • dynamic_display.v
  • btn_debounce.v
  • edge_detect.v

docs.title: Step 2: Write the Top-Level Module
docs.text:
Following Section 3, write hex_counter_top.v:

  • Instantiate the button debounce, edge-detection, counter, and display-driver modules.
  • Important: Connect btn_pulse correctly to counter_mod.en.
  • Set counter_mod.MOD for counting from 0 through 15.
  • Connect count only to digit0; set all other digits to 0.

docs.title: Step 3: Simulation and Verification (Optional)
docs.text:
• Verify that each button event increments the count exactly once. Adjust the debounce parameter to suit the simulation duration.
  • Verify the hexadecimal sequence 0→1→...→9→A→B→C→D→E→F→0.

docs.title: Step 4: Pin Constraints and On-Board Verification
docs.text:
• Use the display constraints.
  • Add a constraint for the button selected as the increment button.
  • Activate only the rightmost digit (an[0]=0, with all other bits set to 1).

docs.title: 5. Questions
docs.text:
Q1: Without modifying counter_mod, how can you change only the top-level connections so that the counter runs from 0 through 9 (decimal) instead of 0 through F?

  • Use a parameterized setting.

Q3: How would you modify the design to display a two-digit hexadecimal value from 0x00 through 0xFF?

Approach:

  • Cascade two counters, one for the low digit and one for the high digit.
  • Low-digit enable = btn_pulse.
  • High-digit enable = the low digit's carry signal.
  • Connect the two count values to two display digits.

Q4: Why use the dynamic_display module instead of driving the display directly?

Analysis:

  • dynamic_display encapsulates the seven-segment drive logic and the mapping of hexadecimal values to glyphs.
  • Modularity improves code reuse and readability.
  • The module supports multiplexed scanning of multiple display digits.

docs.title: Digital Logic: Introduction to Sequential Logic—Counters and Clock Dividers
Objectives
docs.text:
• Master the use of always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n).
  • Learn to design binary and modulo-N counters.
  • Learn to design a clock divider that converts a 100 MHz clock into a required lower-frequency signal.
  • Complete the 1 Hz LED blinking exercise and experience a circuit that changes by itself.

docs.title: 1. Understanding Clock Signals
docs.text:
The EGO1 development board has a 100 MHz crystal oscillator connected to FPGA pin P17. It continuously produces a square wave:

        ┌──┐  ┌──┐  ┌──┐  ┌──┐  ┌──┐
clk:    │  │  │  │  │  │  │  │  │  │
    ────┘  └──┘  └──┘  └──┘  └──┘  └──
        ↑     ↑     ↑     ↑     ↑
      上升沿  上升沿  上升沿  上升沿  上升沿
  • Frequency: 100 MHz, or 100 million cycles per second
  • Period: 10 ns (the waveform repeats every 10 ns)
  • Rising edge: The instant at which the signal changes from 0 to 1

The clock acts as the circuit's “heartbeat.” Our design advances one step at a time on its rising edges.

Constraint-file syntax: 

set_property PACKAGE_PIN P17 [get_ports clk]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports clk]

docs.title: 2. New Syntax: always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
2.1 Basic Form
docs.text:
In previous exercises, always @(*) described a circuit in which an output changed immediately when an input changed. The following construct allows a circuit to change automatically, one clock cycle at a time:

always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n)
        // 复位：把寄存器设为初始值
    else
        // 正常工作：在每个时钟上升沿执行一次
end

Line by line:

  • posedge clk: Execute the operations between begin...end on every rising edge of the clock.
  • negedge rst_n: Execute the reset immediately when rst_n goes low (when the reset button is pressed).
  • if (!rst_n): If the reset signal is low (rst_n = 0), clear all registers or assign their initial values.
  • else: Operate normally while reset is inactive.

docs.title: 2.2 Reset Convention
docs.text:
This course consistently uses an active-low reset, named rst_n (n indicates negative/active-low):

Operation Syntax or value Port declaration input rst_n Sensitivity list always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) Reset condition if (!rst_n) Button pressed on the board rst_n = 0 (reset asserted) Button released rst_n = 1 (normal operation)

The EGO1 development board has a dedicated active-low reset button connected to pin P15, as shown below.

docs.title: 2.3 Assignment Rules
docs.text:
Inside an always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) block, use the non-blocking assignment operator <=:

always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n)
        count <= 4'd0;       // 用 <=
    else
        count <= count + 1;  // 用 <=
end

A simple rule to remember:

  • Combinational always @(*) block → use =
  • Sequential always @(posedge clk ...) block → use <=
  • Do not mix the two.

docs.title: 2.4 The reg Type
docs.text: A signal assigned in an always @(posedge clk ...) block is synthesized into an actual register. It remembers the value from the preceding clock cycle and updates on each clock edge. Therefore, an output assigned in this type of block must be declared as reg.

docs.title: 3.1 4-Bit Binary Counter
docs.text:
The simplest counter increments on every rising edge of the clock:

module counter_4bit (
    input            clk,
    input            rst_n,
    output reg [3:0] count
);
    always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (!rst_n)
            count <= 4'd0;
        else
            count <= count + 1'd1;
    end
endmodule

Behavior: After reset, count = 0. It then increments on every clock edge. After reaching 15, it overflows to 0 and repeats.

docs.title: 3.2 Modulo-N Counter
docs.text:
To return to zero after a particular value—for example, to count from 0 through 9—add a condition:

module counter_mod10 (
    input            clk,
    input            rst_n,
    output reg [3:0] count
);
    always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (!rst_n)
            count <= 4'd0;
        else if (count == 4'd9)
            count <= 4'd0;       // 到9归零
        else
            count <= count + 1'd1;
    end
endmodule

docs.title: 3.3 Parameterized Modulo-N Counter with Enable and Carry
docs.text:
In a practical project, a counter usually needs an enable signal (en) that controls whether it counts and a carry output (carry) for cascading several counters:

module counter_mod #(parameter MOD = 10) (
    input            clk,
    input            rst_n,
    input            en,
    output reg [3:0] count,
    output           carry
);
    assign carry = (count == MOD - 1) && en;

    always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (!rst_n)
            count <= 4'd0;
        else if (en) begin
            if (count == MOD - 1)
                count <= 4'd0;
            else
                count <= count + 1'd1;
        end
    end
endmodule

Example instantiation:

counter_mod #(.MOD(10)) u_cnt10 (
    .clk(clk), .rst_n(rst_n), .en(enable),
    .count(count_out), .carry(carry_out)
);

docs.title: 4.1 Why Do We Need a Clock Divider?
docs.text:
The EGO1 clock operates at 100 MHz (100 million clock cycles per second), but practical applications require much lower rates:

Application Target frequency Required count LED blinking 1 Hz 100,000,000 Seven-segment display scanning ~1 kHz 100,000 Stopwatch time base 100 Hz 1,000,000

A clock divider is a counter that outputs a pulse when it reaches its terminal count.

docs.title: 4.2 Clock Division Principle
docs.text:
To divide 100 MHz down to 1 Hz:

  • 1 Hz means one output pulse per second.
  • A 100 MHz clock has 100 million clock cycles per second.
  • Therefore, output one pulse after counting 100,000,000 cycles.

docs.title: 4.3 Clock Divider Implementation with a Pulse Output
docs.text:
module clk_div #(parameter MAX_COUNT = 100_000_000) (
    input      clk,
    input      rst_n,
    output reg tick      // 分频后的单周期脉冲
);
    reg [31:0] cnt;

    always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (!rst_n) begin
            cnt  <= 32'd0;
            tick <= 1'b0;
        end else if (cnt == MAX_COUNT - 1) begin
            cnt  <= 32'd0;
            tick <= 1'b1;    // 计满，产生一个脉冲
        end else begin
            cnt  <= cnt + 1'd1;
            tick <= 1'b0;    // 其余时刻保持低
        end
    end
endmodule

tick is high for only one clock cycle when the terminal count is reached and remains low at all other times. This is a single-cycle enable pulse.

parameter defines a constant that can be changed when the module is instantiated. The same source code can therefore support different configurations without modification, greatly improving reuse.

Important: Do not use a divided signal as the clock for another module (for example, always @(posedge slow_clk)). All modules should share the system clock clk, with the tick pulse used as an enable.

docs.title: 4.4 Parameterized Examples
docs.text:
// 1Hz —— LED闪烁
clk_div #(.MAX_COUNT(100_000_000)) u_1hz (
    .clk(clk), .rst_n(rst_n), .tick(tick_1hz)
);

// 1kHz —— 数码管扫描
clk_div #(.MAX_COUNT(100_000)) u_1khz (
    .clk(clk), .rst_n(rst_n), .tick(tick_1khz)
);

// 100Hz —— 秒表基准
clk_div #(.MAX_COUNT(1_000_000)) u_100hz (
    .clk(clk), .rst_n(rst_n), .tick(tick_100hz)
);

docs.title: 5.1 Generating a Clock
docs.text:
reg clk;
initial clk = 0;
always #5 clk = ~clk;   // 周期10ns = 100MHz

#5 introduces a 5 ns delay. Toggling the signal every 5 ns produces a clock with a 10 ns period.

docs.title: 5.2 Generating an Active-Low Reset
docs.text:
reg rst_n;
initial begin
    rst_n = 0;      // 一开始按下复位（低有效）
    #25;
    rst_n = 1;      // 松开复位，开始正常工作
end

docs.title: 5.3 Accelerating Simulation
docs.text:
Dividing 100 MHz down to 1 Hz requires simulation of 100 million clock cycles and is extremely slow. Use a much smaller divisor during simulation:

// 仿真时：MAX_COUNT = 10，10个周期就出一个tick
clk_div #(.MAX_COUNT(10)) u_div_sim (
    .clk(clk), .rst_n(rst_n), .tick(tick)
);

docs.title: 5.4 Complete Testbench Example
docs.text:
`timescale 1ns/1ps

module tb_counter_4bit();
    reg        clk;
    reg        rst_n;
    wire [3:0] count;

    // 实例化
    counter_4bit uut (
        .clk   (clk),
        .rst_n (rst_n),
        .count (count)
    );

    // 100MHz 时钟
    initial clk = 0;
    always #5 clk = ~clk;

    // 测试序列
    initial begin
        $monitor("time=%4d: rst_n=%b count=%d", $time, rst_n, count);

        rst_n = 0;          // 复位
        #25;
        rst_n = 1;          // 松开复位，开始计数
        #200;               // 观察计数
        rst_n = 0;          // 再次复位
        #20;
        rst_n = 1;
        #100;
        $finish;
    end
endmodule

docs.title: Exercise 1: LED Blinking at 1 Hz
docs.text: Requirement: Make one LED on the EGO1 blink at 1 Hz (on for 0.5 seconds and off for 0.5 seconds).

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Write the code: Create clk_div.v and led_blink.v.
  2. Simulate and verify: Write a testbench, change the division factor to 10, and inspect the tick and led transition waveforms.
  3. Assign pins and verify on the board:
  4. clk → P17 (100 MHz crystal oscillator)
  5. rst_n → P15 (reset button)
  6. led → Assign to one LED
  7. Synthesize, generate the bitstream, and program the board, then observe the LED blinking.

docs.title: Exercise 2 (Optional): 4-Bit Binary Counter with LED Output
docs.text: Requirement: Use four LEDs to display a 4-bit binary counter that increments once per second.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Write the code: Use a clock divider to generate a 1 Hz pulse. Increment the 4-bit counter on each pulse and connect its value to four LEDs.
  2. Simulate and verify: Verify the repeating sequence 0→1→2→...→15→0.
  3. Verify on the board: Observe the LEDs displaying the count in binary, with one complete cycle taking approximately 16 seconds.

Question: What must be changed to make the counter count only from 0 through 9 (modulo 10)?

docs.title: Appendix: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text:
• Q: What happens when the counter overflows? A: A 4-bit counter ([3:0]) automatically returns to 0 when incremented after 15. To return to zero after a specific value, add an if (count == target_value) condition.

  • Q: Why does the clock divider produce no pulse in simulation? A: Check whether the simulation runs long enough. During simulation, use a small division factor such as MAX_COUNT = 10 instead of simulating 100 million cycles.

  • Q: Can the output of a clock divider be used directly as a clock? A: This is strongly discouraged. An FPGA design should use a single global clock, clk, and use the divider's tick pulse as an enable. Multiple clocks introduce clock-domain-crossing problems and are a common source of errors.

  • Q: Why use rst_n (active-low) instead of rst (active-high)? A: The reset button on the EGO1 development board outputs a low level while pressed and a high level when released. An active-low reset matches this hardware behavior: pressing the button resets the circuit, and releasing it resumes normal operation.
